Quick recap from last lesson before today's sound challenges start.

items.prompt: Increasing the colour depth of an image mainly gives you...
options: A smaller file, with fewer colours
A larger file, with more possible colours
A larger image, with the same colours
items.explain: More bits per pixel means more possible colour values (2^depth), at the cost of a larger file.

items.prompt: Image resolution is best described as...
options: The number of colours an image can use
The number of pixels used to make up the image
How compressed the image file is
items.explain: Resolution is the number of pixels (width x height) used to represent the image - not colours, not compression.

steps.label: Sound Lab
steps.content:
Data Representation

Sound Lab

Year 10, 1.2 L3 · Sound · 30 minutes

  • Concept: How a computer turns a continuous sound wave into stored numbers.
  • Challenge 1: Drag the sample rate and watch (and hear) the recording fall apart.
  • Challenge 2: Do the same with sample resolution.
  • Challenge 3: Free play with both, and listen to the difference for yourself.
  • Real world: Compare CD audio, phone calls and voice memos.

steps.label: What Is Sound, Digitally?
steps.content:
What Is Sound, Digitally?

A real sound - your voice, a guitar string, a car horn - is a continuous wave: air pressure changing smoothly, with no gaps and no fixed steps. A computer can only store numbers, so it has to turn that smooth wave into a list of them.

It does this by sampling: measuring the height of the wave at regular instants in time, then rounding each measurement to the nearest value it can actually store. Two settings control how faithful that recording is:

  • Sample rate - how many measurements are taken per second. Too few, and fast changes in the wave get missed entirely.
  • Sample resolution - how many bits are used to store each measurement. Too few, and every measurement gets rounded to a nearby value that is only roughly right.

Both of these work exactly like resolution and colour depth did for images last lesson - more of either means a more faithful copy of the original, and a bigger file.

steps.label: Challenge 3: Free Play and Listen
steps.content:
Challenge 3: Free Play and Listen

Both sliders are unlocked. File size in bits/sec = sample rate × sample resolution. Try to find the lowest settings where the tone is still clearly recognisable - then press Play to check by ear, not just by eye.

steps.label: Real-World Sample Rates
steps.content:
Real-World Sample Rates

The same trade-off you just explored decides the settings real recording formats actually use:

FormatSample rateSample resolutionWhy
Telephone call8,000 Hz8-bitSpeech is still understandable at low quality, and it keeps the amount of data sent very small.
Voice memo / podcast44,100 Hz16-bitClear speech and music without an enormous file.
CD audio44,100 Hz16-bitThe standard for near-transparent music quality.
Studio recording96,000 Hz24-bitExtra headroom for editing and mixing before the final release.

Notice a phone call uses a much lower sample rate than music - a smaller file matters more than perfect quality when speech only needs to be understood, not enjoyed.

y10_1_2_l3_examterm.feedback: This is the single measurement itself - not how often it is taken (that is the rate) and not how it is stored (that is the resolution).

y10_1_2_l3_exambinary.feedback: Add up the place values for each 1 - the same method you used in 1.1.
Same method as before - add up the place values for each 1 in this byte.
Split the byte into its two nibbles and convert each nibble to hex separately.
The leading 1 means this is negative - invert the bits and add 1, the same as in 1.1, then remember the minus sign.

y10_1_2_l3_practice.feedback: Multiply the sample rate by the sample resolution, the same way you multiplied width, height and colour depth for images.
Bit depth and number of levels are connected by a power of 2 - the same relationship as colour depth and number of colours.
Think about what a higher sample rate lets the recording keep that a lower one would miss - and what that does to the file.
Compare what a phone call actually needs (to be understood) against what a music recording needs (to sound good), and what that does to file size or bandwidth.
Multiply the sample rate by the sample resolution, the same way you did for part (a).

y10_1_2_l3_plenary.feedback: Think about what is being counted, and over what unit of time.
Think about what is being measured for each individual sample, not the recording as a whole.
This works the same way increasing colour depth did for images last lesson - think about accuracy and file size together.
Work out the bits for one second first, then scale that up for the full length of the recording.
